structure.title: Act I · Rome celebrates · Who may have a triumph?
structure.text: Tradesmen take the day off to watch Caesar, while officials question their sudden change of allegiance. Cassius picks his moment to ask what Brutus sees when he looks at Caesar. Rome's future begins as an argument about another man's appearance.

structure.title: Act II – Act III, scene 1 · A private decision becomes a public killing
structure.text: In his orchard Brutus tries to reason from what Caesar might become. The conspirators need his name on an act already being planned. Warnings reaching Caesar on the way to the Capitol compete with his need to appear unafraid.

structure.title: Act III, scene 2 – Act V · After the speeches · Who commands an army?
structure.text: In the forum Brutus and Antony each get a hearing. Then the city divides and the action moves into soldiers' tents. A man who could once rely upon his friend's honour now needs money, supplies and joint decisions about where to march.

people.name: Brutus and Cassius
people.text: Cassius can identify a vulnerable moment and recruit the people to exploit it. Brutus's reputation can give their enterprise a dignity Cassius knows he cannot supply himself. Their disagreements begin before they draw their weapons.

people.name: Antony
people.role: Caesar's friend and a gifted public speaker
people.text: The conspirators must decide how much harm a loyal friend could possibly do once the chief danger is gone. Antony understands what it means to stand beside a body while addressing people who can see it.

people.name: Portia and Calpurnia
people.text: Both sense danger inside a marriage and try to influence what their husbands do in public. Each conversation tests how much a Roman husband believes he must conceal to be worthy of his name.

context.title: Why a crown alarms Rome
context.text: Romans who prize the republic associate kingship with submission to one family's will. Killing a ruler in the name of freedom leaves open the difficult practical question of who gets to speak for the people the following morning.

notice.text: Follow the evidence offered for a future crime.
notice.why: Brutus's most important argument concerns what Caesar might do with greater power. Observations about the present have to bear the weight of a hypothetical future.

notice.text: What do the citizens ask for during the funeral?
notice.why: At first they want reasons, then particular words and objects. The movement of a crowd can be heard in changes to the questions a speaker is being invited to answer.

opening: Brutus loves Caesar and fears what he might become. Persuaded that Rome’s freedom is at stake, he joins men planning to kill his friend before he can make himself a tyrant. Brutus believes his reasons will be enough to justify the deed to the people. But a city does not interpret a killing as neatly as a conspirator explains it, and Shakespeare gives the men fighting over Caesar’s legacy a weapon Brutus has dangerously underestimated: the power to tell the crowd what it has seen.
